title: Statistics: are Stehle's DIAWINFBN run and the mod-7 doublets real?
why: Two famous K4 oddities nobody has put a corrected p-value on. Cheap; tells us whether to chase 4- or 7-spaced structure.

title: Sanborn's 2025 hints as keywords everywhere (Quagmire I-IV + theme-keyword columnar x all key models)
why: Newest clues (Egypt 1986, Berlin Wall, delivering a message, World Clock) are barely mined.

title: Decimation (97 is prime), grid routes, K3 rotations x every key model
why: Others tried these scrambles with repeating keys only; progressive, autokey and digit keys behind them are untested.

title: Myszkowski from ~190k dictionary words x every key model
why: Myszkowski was only covered at widths 3-9 with a periodic key.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-11) + digit / small-shift key
why: Digit keys are dead alone but untested behind a transposition; fits Bean's 'letters sit close' finding.

title: Double columnar (widths 2-6 x 2-6) x progressive / autokey / digit keys
why: Attack 07 did double columnar with periodic keys only.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-10) + autokey (ciphertext or plaintext feeds the key)
why: Autokey alone is dead; stacked behind a transposition it is untested.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-10) + progressive key
why: Progressive alone is dead; stacked it is untested.

title: Keyword alphabets at key lengths 14-26, forced plaintext scored for English
why: Clue letters can't decide these lengths (open gap); English scoring against shuffled K4 can.

title: Double columnar width 8 x widths 2-6 + periodic key
why: Pushes attack 07 one width further.

title: Fingerprint ranking: which cipher families produce K4-like statistics?
why: No key search. Ranks ~30 families by how often their output shows K4's oddities (flat IoC, lag-4 run, mod-7 doublets, width-21 repeats, close letters), as a soft prior for where to search next.

title: Practice puzzles: decrypt PK1-PK9 from the public keys, test our blind solvers
why: Ground truth for calibration: shows how far our toolkit reaches on Paradigm's idea of 'Kryptos-like' ciphers.

title: Quagmire I/II (one hidden alphabet) at every key length; undecidable lengths completed by annealing
why: Lengths 13, 16, 19, 20, 23, 24, 26 can't be decided by the clues (open gap); English completion vs planted and shuffled controls can.

title: Gromark / chain-addition keys with both alphabets hidden; survivors completed by annealing
why: A top fingerprint family. Bean's 39 survivors 'can be completed several ways' - this does the completion and compares with controls.

title: Fingerprint ranking again, with the new hidden-alphabet families
why: Do Gromark-with-hidden-alphabets and Quagmire I/II/IV look K4-like?

title: LAYER TWO: two stacked repeating keys, every length pair <=26, completed by annealing
why: Stacked keys (PK3/PK8 style, K2's 'LAYER TWO') give a key that never repeats inside 97 letters on a plain alphabet. The undecidable pairs were never completed.

title: Three layers: a theme word plus two unknown keys (fully clue-determined configs)
why: PK8 stacked four keys; with one layer a known theme word the rest is exactly solvable.

title: K1-K3 misspellings (L/Q, O/U, E/A, S/C) as alphabet swaps x key models and two stacked keys
why: Sanborn: K1-K3 answers hold clues and the misspellings are deliberate; as alphabet swaps they give the near-plain alphabets our fingerprint favours. Untested in this form.

title: World Clock (Weltzeituhr) as of 1989: city names, initials and UTC offsets as keys
why: Sanborn (2025): BERLINCLOCK = the World Clock at Alexanderplatz and the 1989 Wall fall matters. Everyone used the post-1997 plates; we reconstructed the 1989 ones from dated photos.

title: Visual letter transforms: semaphore rotations/mirrors and Morse reverse/invert, alone or stacked with key layers
why: Sanborn's 'visual systems'; semaphore is two hands on a dial (Berlin Clock-shaped). Never tested.

title: Compass-bearing keys read across the exact carved layout (cipher panel, tableau, mirrored tableau)
why: EAST NORTHEAST is in the clue; physical/visual steps; uses the verified carved line layout.

title: SLM cipher detective: small neural net trained on ~100k synthetic K4-like ciphertexts names K4's family
why: A learned, richer version of the fingerprint ranking; training on K4 itself can't work (97 letters).

title: Local LLM (Qwen2.5-7B) as English judge for the blind stacked-key region, plus what it generates as K4
why: Quadgrams can't tell real from fake English where ~20 key letters are free; an LLM judge might, calibrated on planted vs shuffled.

title: Key-shape forensics: period signatures in letter differences; could the key be a slowly turning dial?
why: NSA's 'pattern every 7', the mod-7 doublets, Bean's width 21 and the neural detective's 'progressive' all hint at key shape.

title: Self-masking: K4 keyed by its own plaintext or ciphertext read in a scrambled order
why: Scheidt's 'masking' on a plain alphabet; natural-order self-keying (autokey) is dead, scrambled never tried.

title: Baudot/Vernam teleprinter cipher (ITA2 XOR): periodic, stacked, autokey, word and text keys
why: K2's 'transmitted underground' = the CIA Berlin Tunnel tapping teleprinter lines; never tested on K4.

title: Lorenz-style teleprinter wheels: each of the 5 bits with its own short repeating wheel
why: The Cold War teleprinter machine family; each bit plane is exactly testable on its own.

title: Paper strips: K4's carved rows or equal-width strips, reordered and flipped, x every key model
why: Kobek found the plaintext as strips taped out of order; the verified carved layout gives the strips.

title: Egypt-era alphabets (hieroglyph, Coptic, Greek, Phoenician, Arabic orders) x key models, Quagmire, stacked keys
why: Sanborn: the 1986 Egypt trip figures in the solution; near-plain alphabets are what the fingerprint favours.

title: Shifting matrices / number-base change: grid coordinates each shifted by its own wheel
why: Sanborn: 'matrix codes Ed gave me'; Scheidt: 'a different math base', 'shifting matrices'. Only the base-3 cube with simple keys was tried.

title: Gromark in other number bases (3-16), both alphabets hidden, completed
why: Scheidt's 'different math base'; Bean/Barney list survivors in base 8 etc.; completions never done.

title: Long stacked keys revisited: heat-bath solver + English-key prior
why: Diagnosis showed the open region is search-limited (true answers score higher than what was found), not information-limited.

title: Selective masking: KRYPTOS letters lightly shifted, the rest keyed
why: 9/10 KRYPTOS-letter clues shift <=2 (shuffled p~0.003); maybe the keyword decides which letters get the real key.

title: Key restarts at each sentence (+X separators), 18 alphabets
why: Plaintext = sentence strips; K1-K3 use X between sentences; Cyrillic Projector restarts its key per block.

title: A different simple system for each part (split 34-63)
why: 'Two separate systems' read literally: one for the EASTNORTHEAST part, another for the BERLINCLOCK part.

title: One deliberate mistake: drop-one-clue for periodic, two keys, hidden-alphabet Gromark
why: Sanborn's work is 'rife with mistakes on purpose'; one wrong clue letter makes exact tests reject the true method.

title: KRYPTOS-letter masking inside the clue sentences + restarting key (pre-filter hybrid)
why: Clue matrix: selective masking explains the KRYPTOS closeness but breaks flatness unless <=~20 letters are masked; top hybrid = masking x sentence restarts.

title: Two stacked keys that are both real words/phrases/dates (+ one-wrong-clue pass)
why: Round 6: long stacked keys are information-limited; hand keys are words (PALIMPSEST, ABSCISSA), which removes every free slot.

title: Three layers: theme word + two word keys
why: Same, with a theme word (Berlin/Egypt/clock/K1-K3) as a third layer; three-stage stacks are a listed community gap.

title: K1-K3 plaintexts as keys with hidden alphabets (4 models)
why: 'Answers to K1-K3 contain clues to K4'; text keys were only tried on A-Z/KRYPTOS alphabets.

title: Clock arithmetic keys (dials 12/24/60, two hands) + carved-row restarts
why: 'Delve into that particular clock': a clock is modular arithmetic; carved row 4 restarts inside BERLINCLOCK, which idea 43 couldn't test.

title: Letter class picks the table (KRYPTOS letters on the KRYPTOS tableau)
why: KRYPTOS-letter clues behave differently; two tables by letter class is a fully keyed version that can stay flat.

title: Second look at every saved candidate (big model, word coverage, LLM judge)
why: Every candidate was judged by one score at the time; re-judge all together, calibrated on real English with forced clues.

title: Formula mining: every 0-4 ingredient linear formula for the key
why: Earlier rounds tested named key rules one at a time; this tests every short combination of 186 ingredients at once.

title: Autokey / Condi / Ragbaby with a hidden alphabet (exact linear solve)
why: Autokey was only ruled out on known alphabets; the hidden alphabet drops out of a linear system mod 26.

title: Interrupted key: restart at a trigger letter or at each word
why: A classical hand cipher that hides the period; restarts were only tested at sentences and carved rows.

title: Sentence key (unknown English text) on keyword tableaux
why: K1/K2's own system with a different keyword and a whole-sentence key; the forced key letters must read as English.

title: The sculpture read other ways as the key (columns, diagonals, skips)
why: Sanborn's step is 'visual'; sculpture running keys were only read along the rows.

title: Autokey stacked with a repeating key word (two systems)
why: The two simplest in-place hand systems stacked directly; only tested behind transpositions before.

title: Two systems in turn: switching rows, interleaved streams, Slidefair pairs
why: Three literal readings of 'two separate systems' that round 7 did not cover.

title: Scrambled key: K3's transposition applied to the repeating key, text left in place
why: Uses both of the lower half's systems while keeping BERLINCLOCK in place, which text transpositions cannot.

title: Drifting key word (each key letter steps at its own rate) + the EAST/EAST near-repeat measured
why: EAST encrypts to FLRV and, 9 letters on, to GKSS: nearly the same. Tests the model that suggests.

title: Three remembered key words: Quagmire IV over all dictionary alphabet pairs (hash join)
why: Scheidt: simple, remembered, 'with the correct key word/s'. K1/K2's machine with three words instead of two.

title: The '?' counts: 98 = 7 x 14 cells (reruns of 54, 61, 62 with KRYPTOS_QMARK=1)
why: Scheidt: special characters must be accounted for. With the ? K4 is an exact grid; 97 alone is prime.

title: Chain-addition key in letters; row word + column word grids
why: Ways an agent stretches a remembered word into a long key; clue blocks start 42 apart = K3 worksheet width.

title: Every dictionary keyword tableau x battery of key rules (sliding, stacked, autokey...)
why: Round 9's key rules were only run on the A-Z and KRYPTOS tableaux; the tableau keyword may be another word.

title: Carter's reply as a guessed third clue; undecided models re-run
why: K3 ends with a question and K4 starts where the answer would; 18 more letters make undecidable models decidable.

title: Each clue alone, and both clues with the gap off by 1-3 letters
why: Sanborn dropped a letter carving K2; every joint test assumes the 42-letter gap between the clues is exact.

title: Rows of 21: column key shared by the two clue rows, row decides offset or tableau
why: Both clues start a row in a 21-wide grid (K3's worksheet was 42 wide); 'ID BY ROWS'.

title: Wrong modulus: key arithmetic on a wheel of 27-31 cells
why: Scheidt: special characters must be accounted for (27 symbols with '?'); the carved tableau rows are 30-31 wide.

title: Multiplier word + adder word (C = A*P + B, both repeating)
why: Decimated alphabets are as easy by hand as shifted ones; only one fixed multiplier had been allowed.

title: Paper rotor: hidden wiring between two alphabets, turned by a key word
why: Not linear in a hidden alphabet, so unseen by every earlier exact test; others tried only constant-speed rotors.

title: Evolving alphabet: the alphabet changes after every letter
why: A one-sentence hand rule with flat statistics and no period; decrypts from letter 0 with no unknown plaintext.

title: Autokey with a keyed distance (a pattern says how far back to look)
why: All earlier autokey tests used one fixed lag.

title: Wheatstone clock-face cipher with any rings (proof + dictionary cross-check)
why: BERLIN CLOCK, a 27th symbol; the repeated cipher letters S,S and R,R decide it for every ring.

title: Digital interpretation: letters as 5 bits (binary, Gray, Bacon), Morse as a switch
why: DIGETAL INTERPRETATU; only Baudot numbering had been tested.

title: Tableau seen through the pierced copper: mirrored, flipped, slanted overlays
why: SHADOW FORCES, 'it's visual'; round 9 read the panels as text but not as a mirrored overlay.

title: Round 11 battery (68 clue alone / gap slack, 70 mod 27-31, 71B fixed multipliers, 74 keyed-lag autokey) on 446,675 transposition-mixed keyword alphabets
why: Ideas 68, 70, 71 and 74 used the 220k plain keyword alphabets; round 10 showed the two transposition-mixed forms triple the alphabet set and are how a keyword alphabet is often built by hand.

title: German sentence keys on keyword tableaux: not run, the repository has no German language model
why: BERLIN CLOCK and the 1989 Berlin setting make German text a natural running key; attack 57 scored forced key fragments only against English.

title: Gap between the clues off by 1-3 letters: formula mining (54, sizes 0-3) and the three-keyword Quagmire IV hash join (63, key lengths 1-20)
why: Idea 68 showed nothing with the gap between the clues off by 1-3 letters, but only for the key-rule battery. Formula mining (54) and the Quagmire IV hash join (63) also tie the two clues together through absolute positions.

title: One wrong clue letter: key-rule battery, multiplier+adder words (71A) and word-turned rotor (72) on every 23 of the 24 clue letters
why: Sanborn's texts carry deliberate misspellings (IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND, DESPARATLY). Round 7 tested one wrong clue letter only for periodic, two-key and Gromark models.

title: Two paper rotors in series: two different hidden wirings (form H, mostly cannot be judged) and one hidden strip used there and back (form B, dead)
why: Idea 72 closed one rotor with hidden wiring. Two rotors is the smallest machine that idea cannot see, and the wire-collision test extends to it when the slow rotor moves rarely.

title: Any state machine moved by a hidden table of the letter (cipher = F(state), state += g(letter) mod m, m = 2..60): the plain pair S,T is doubled once and not doubled once
why: The Wheatstone proof (idea 75) used only this: plain S then T gives cipher S,S at letters 32-33, and plain S ... T gives cipher R,R at letters 23 and 28. Any state machine must treat T after S,T,N,O,R as it treated S.

title: Two repeating-key layers on two different tableaux (A-Z, KRYPTOS, theme and dictionary keyword alphabets), exact test on the clue letters
why: K2 ends LAYER TWO and Scheidt calls K4 'more than one stage'. Every stacked-key test so far put both layers on the same tableau, where the two keys simply add. A KRYPTOS-tableau layer followed by an A-Z layer (or any two different keyword tableaux) is not a sum of keys on any single alphabet, so none of the earlier exact tests can see it.

title: K4 letters as skip counts through the sculpture's own text: moving window (rule A) and pointer walk (rule B) over 39 texts
why: Sanborn 2019: no particular book is needed, 'just to be able to read'; 2025: 'Who says it is even a math solution?'; 2005-2006: the earlier passages hold instructions and clues for the fourth. A reading method fits all three: each K4 letter says how far to count on (A=1..Z=26) through K1-K3 to reach the next plaintext letter. The encoder can choose among occurrences, which flattens the letter counts (masking) and lets S give S. Every earlier test treats the cipher letter as a letter added to a key, never as a distance.
